title: The Ahluwalia misl
hookLine: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's misl, later the state of Kapurthala

cards: Two hats. That was today's chief's problem. You've met Jassa Singh Ahluwalia on this path already: the boy who sang kirtan, the young rider Nawab Kapur Singh trained, the man the Khalsa called Sultan-ul-Qaum.
Today, a different side. He had his own band, with its own riders and villages to look after. And he was the one the chiefs looked to when all the bands rode together.
Lead your own people, and lead everyone. Today: the Ahluwalia misl.

teach.b: Four pieces. The name: tradition says Jassa Singh's family came from a village called Ahlu, near Lahore, and his band took its name from it, Ahluwalia, the ones from Ahlu.

The first hat: as chief of his own misl, he had riders who had chosen to ride with him and villages that looked to his band for protection. That's a sardar's ordinary work: keep your people fed, safe and together.

teach.h: AT THE HEAD OF THE DAL KHALSA.
teach.b: The second hat: tradition says that when the bands gathered at Amritsar and rode as the Dal Khalsa, the chiefs put Jassa Singh at the head. Think what that asks of a man.

When spoils are shared, does his own band get the best? When there's a hard job, does it go to someone else's riders? In the way Sikh histories tell it, the other chiefs trusted him, and that trust is the whole point.
A leader of everyone can't lead only for his own. Last, what the band became.
Long after the riding years, the lands of the Ahluwalia misl became the state of Kapurthala, ruled by chiefs who carried the Ahluwalia name. The band outlasted the age of bands.
Other misls are remembered for a fort, a flag, a river or a fight. This one is remembered for who led it, and because he was trusted beyond it.

how: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader of the Dal Khalsa, and the Ahluwalia name lives on in families and in the town of Kapurthala.

games.q: you're Jassa Singh, at the head of the Dal Khalsa. the spoils of a campaign are being shared among the bands. your own riders are watching. what do you do?
o: give your own band the best share.
share fairly, so the other chiefs keep trusting you.
send it all to Amritsar and let no band share.
games.why: in the way Sikh histories tell it, the chiefs of other bands trusted him. a leader of everyone can't lead only for his own.

practice: Bring to mind someone who led you well, up close: a coach, a manager, a teacher, an older cousin. Notice whether they were fair to people who weren't their own, and what made you trust them.
On each breath, be thankful for one thing they did, with Waheguru on the breath out if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Jassa Singh, whose band from Ahlu became the Ahluwalia misl. This week: chardi kala in the century, the women who kept the homes, what the century teaches, the hard century's close, the misl, the Bhangis, and the Ahluwalias. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Ahluwalia: 'of Ahlu', the village the misl was named for.
